path/path-map.alt: The complete curriculum: twenty-one weeks, sixty-three published sessions, three acts and twelve units. The completion flag marks Session 12.5.
path/path-map.caption: The route: 21 weeks, three acts, the flag marks the latest written session.

session-3-1/fig1-three-containers.alt: Three vessels for a value: a green let jar and a yellow const flask drawn inside a dashed block, let refilled from 100 to 75 with a tick, const refused with a TypeError; a red var cauldron outside the block labelled function-scoped and hoisted, with an arrow reading leaks out
session-3-1/fig1-three-containers.caption: Three ways to hold mana. let and const stay inside their block; var leaks out of the braces and is hoisted to undefined.

session-3-1/fig2-seven-primitives.alt: Seven cards, string, number, boolean, undefined, null, symbol, bigint, each with an example value and its typeof answer in green; the null card is outlined in red because typeof null answers object, marked as a 1995 bug
session-3-1/fig2-seven-primitives.caption: The seven primitives and what typeof says about each. Only null lies, and it has been lying since 1995.

session-3-1/fig3-two-passes.alt: Two panels. Pass 1, registration: var ghost is set to undefined, let hero is locked in the temporal dead zone, function cast is ready. Pass 2, execution: console.log(ghost) prints undefined silently, console.log(hero) throws a ReferenceError, cast() works before its declaration line
session-3-1/fig3-two-passes.caption: Hoisting is two passes. Declarations are registered first; then the lines run in order. var reads as undefined early, let and const throw.

session-3-1/fig4-branching-road.alt: A flowchart of an if, else if, else chain for playerHP equal to 75: the first test, greater than 50, is taken along a solid green arrow to You are healthy; the other three tests are dimmed with dashed arrows; a side panel lists the six falsy values, false, 0, empty string, null, undefined and NaN
session-3-1/fig4-branching-road.caption: The branching road. Only the first true test is taken, so order matters; the six falsy values decide what counts as true at each gate.

session-3-1/fig5-two-equals-signs.alt: Two columns of comparisons. Under a red double equals, 5 equals string 5, empty string equals false, 0 equals string 0, null equals undefined and empty array equals false are all true. Under a green triple equals every one of them is false. A strip below shows string 5 plus 3 giving 53, string 5 minus 3 giving 2, and true plus 1 giving 2
session-3-1/fig5-two-equals-signs.caption: Two equals signs lie. == converts before it compares; === never converts. Plus glues strings while minus converts them.

session-3-2/fig1-three-spellings.alt: Three rows, Declaration, Expression and Arrow, each showing the same calculateDamage function written that way; ticks and crosses beside each note hoisted or not hoisted, own this or no this of its own, and implicit return for the arrow; a strip below contrasts calculateDamage(25, 10) giving 15 with the bare name giving a Function
session-3-2/fig1-three-spellings.caption: One spell, three spellings. Declarations are hoisted; expressions and arrows are not; arrows have no this of their own. Parentheses cast the spell, the bare name is the scroll.

session-3-2/fig2-scope-rings.alt: Three nested rounded rings labelled global scope with worldName, function scope enterDungeon with dungeonLevel, and block scope with boss and loot; beside them five lookups, three green ones reading outward succeed and two red ones reading boss after the block or dungeonLevel outside the function throw a ReferenceError
session-3-2/fig2-scope-rings.caption: The scope chain. Lookups walk outward through the rings and never inward; var ignores the innermost ring entirely.

session-3-2/fig3-backpack.alt: A dashed, faded createCounter function marked finished and gone; to its right two returned functions each carrying a small backpack icon with count inside, hitCounter on 3 after three calls returning 1, 2, 3, and comboCounter on 1 after one call
session-3-2/fig3-backpack.caption: The backpack. The outer call is over; the inner function left carrying count. Every call to the factory packs a new backpack, and nothing outside can open one.

session-3-2/fig4-combo-chain.alt: Four stages joined by green arrows: heroes, five object cards; filter power greater than 8000, the same five with two struck through; map to power, three numbers 9001, 8200 and 8500; reduce with a sum, 0 plus the three numbers equals 25701
session-3-2/fig4-combo-chain.caption: The combo chain. filter keeps fewer, map keeps the count but changes the shape, reduce folds to one value; the original array is untouched the whole way.

session-3-2/fig5-missing-return.alt: Three panels titled costume one the forgotten word, costume two braces without return, and costume three map with a block body; each shows red code producing undefined or an array of undefined, then the green one-line fix producing 5, 8, and the array of names
session-3-2/fig5-missing-return.caption: The missing return in its three costumes. A function with no return hands back undefined; braces make a block, so an arrow with braces needs the word.

session-3-5/fig1-file-and-tree.alt: Left, the index.html source as text in a panel; a green arrow; right, the same page as a tree of boxes: document at the root, then html, head with title, body with h3 main-title, p subtitle, div container holding two p.message, button change-btn and ul quest-list holding three li
session-3-5/fig1-file-and-tree.caption: The file and the tree. The browser parses index.html once and builds the DOM; JavaScript changes the tree in memory and never the file on disk.

session-3-5/fig2-three-selectors.alt: Three rows: getElementById subtitle lights up one node and returns one element; querySelector .message lights up only the first of two matching nodes; querySelectorAll .message lights up both and returns a NodeList, with notes that the first two return null when nothing matches and that a NodeList needs Array.from for map
session-3-5/fig2-three-selectors.caption: Three selectors. By id and querySelector hand back one element or null; querySelectorAll hands back every match as a NodeList, which has forEach but not map.

session-3-5/fig3-four-dials.alt: Four cards, textContent, innerHTML marked careful, classList and style, each with the line of code and a before and after of the element's markup: text replaced, tags parsed in, classes added, inline style written; a footer names setAttribute and removeAttribute for everything else
session-3-5/fig3-four-dials.caption: Four dials on every element. textContent for text, innerHTML only for markup you wrote yourself, classList for state the stylesheet styles, style for one-off inline rules.

session-3-5/fig4-event-delegation.alt: Nested boxes document, body and ul quest-list; inside the list four items, one highlighted as the clicked event.target and one dashed as added later; a single addEventListener badge on the ul; to the right the bubbling path li to ul to body to document and the delegation code using event.target.matches
session-3-5/fig4-event-delegation.caption: Event delegation. A click bubbles up from the element to the document; one listener on the parent hears every child, including children created after the listener was attached.

session-3-5/fig5-null-and-reload.alt: Two timelines: a script in the head running before the body is parsed, getElementById returning null and a TypeError, fixed with defer or moving the script to the end of body; and a form submit whose default action reloads the page and erases every variable, fixed with event.preventDefault as the first line of the handler
session-3-5/fig5-null-and-reload.caption: Null and the reload. The script ran before the tree existed, or the form's default action rebuilt the page; both feel like code that does nothing.

session-3-4/fig1-hand-copied.alt: A grid of many small player cards, each with a name, hp and its own red attack function block; a counter reads 500 players, 500 copies of attack, one bug fixed 500 times
session-3-4/fig1-hand-copied.caption: Five hundred hand-copied players. Every card carries its own copy of attack(), so one bug is five hundred fixes.

session-3-4/fig2-blueprint.alt: A yellow blueprint sheet labelled class Character listing takeDamage, heal, attackTarget; three arrows labelled new lead to three small cards, Warrior, Mage, Healer, each holding only name, hp and attack values
session-3-4/fig2-blueprint.caption: One blueprint. The instances hold their own fields; the methods live once, on the class, and every instance reaches them.

session-3-4/fig3-prototype-chain.alt: Four linked boxes in a row, conan, Warrior.prototype, Character.prototype, Object.prototype, ending at null; a green path labelled berserk stops at the first box; a yellow path labelled toString walks all the way to Object.prototype; a red x marks null
session-3-4/fig3-prototype-chain.caption: The prototype chain. conan.berserk() is found one hop up; conan.toString() walks to the top and finds it on Object.prototype; the chain ends at null.

session-3-4/fig4-this-loses-character.alt: Four panels: method call, this is the hero object; plain call, a lone function with this undefined and a red question mark; bind, a rope ties the function back to hero; new, a fresh empty object. The arrow-function note says arrows have no this of their own
session-3-4/fig4-this-loses-character.caption: The four rules of this. Rule 2 is the bug: a method pulled off its object loses its character.

session-3-6/fig1-game-loop.alt: Five boxes in a row joined by green arrows: event (click, keydown, submit, tick), handler (guard, update state, render), state (board, turn, winner, score, timer, lives), render() (renderBoard, renderScore, renderMessage) and DOM (what the player sees); a loop-back line under them reads the player sees the new screen and acts again
session-3-6/fig1-game-loop.caption: The game loop. An event arrives, the handler guards and updates state, render() writes the DOM, the player reacts, and the loop turns again. State is the only source of truth.

session-3-6/fig2-single-source-of-truth.alt: Two panels of wrong and right code: rule one, the DOM is a display not a database, contrasts parseInt of scoreEl.textContent with state.score += 1 then render(); rule two, never store what you can compute, contrasts a moveCount variable with isTie computed from board.every; below, three one-line habits: constants, grouped state, cached elements
session-3-6/fig2-single-source-of-truth.caption: The rules of the arena. Never read game data back out of the DOM, never keep a second copy of something you can compute, and name your magic numbers.

session-3-6/fig3-skeleton-and-order.alt: Left, an app.js file with five labelled comment sections: constants, state variables, cached DOM elements, event listeners, functions, each with one or two example lines; right, seven numbered steps in the proven order, from declaring state through init and render to handlers, ending with commit at every milestone in yellow
session-3-6/fig3-skeleton-and-order.caption: The skeleton and the order. Five sections in every game file, and the seven steps that take you from an empty file to a working first screen without stalling.

session-3-6/fig4-timer-leak.alt: Left, a table of seconds: Start at 0 s begins interval one, Start again at 2 s begins interval two while one is still alive, then two ticks a second until the timer passes zero and Game Over prints every second in red; right, the three-line fix: a guard on isPlaying, clearInterval before setInterval, and clearInterval again in endGame
session-3-6/fig4-timer-leak.caption: The interval that never died. Start pressed twice means two timers; nothing cleared them, so the game over fires forever. Keep the id and clear it on restart and on end.

session-3-6/fig5-four-arenas.alt: Four cards lettered A to D: Memory Card Game with class Card, Whack-a-Mole with class Mole, Quiz Game with class Quiz, RPG Battle with Character, Player, Enemy and Battle; each card lists the state it tracks, a green win condition, a red lose condition and the utilities it leans on, such as shuffle, setInterval or Math.max
session-3-6/fig5-four-arenas.caption: Four arenas. Each option is the same loop with a different state list; the card tells you the class you will write, what you must track, and how the game is won and lost.

session-1-1/fig1-terminal-shell-conversa.alt: Left, a terminal window drawn with three dots and a yellow border labelled the terminal, the window you open; inside it a green-bordered box labelled the shell, bash or zsh, the interpreter inside it, showing echo Hello World, pwd, whoami and ls with their answers and a blinking cursor; right, four numbered steps of the conversation: you type and press Enter, the shell reads the first word as the command, it finds and runs the program, the program prints and a new prompt appears
session-1-1/fig1-terminal-shell-conversa.caption: The terminal is the window, the shell is the language it speaks, and every command is the same four-step conversation. Console is just another name for the same experience.

session-1-1/fig2-command-anatomy.alt: A card with the template command [options] [arguments] in yellow, green and white, then four real lines coloured by role: ls -la my-website, mkdir -p projects/isekai/unit-01, echo "# My Website" > README.md with the arrow in red, and touch index.html style.css app.js; under each piece a tiny label says command, option, argument or redirect, and a note on the right says what the line does
session-1-1/fig2-command-anatomy.caption: Every line has the same shape: what to do, how to do it, what to do it to. Options start with a dash; square brackets mean optional; a space splits arguments, which is why names with spaces break.

session-1-1/fig3-camp-tree.alt: Left, seven commands in order: mkdir -p isekai-camp/inventory/weapons, two more mkdir -p lines for armor, potions, main-story and side-quests, plain mkdir for journal, touch for wooden-sword.txt, then echo with > and echo with >> into journal/day-01.txt; right, the tree they produce: isekai-camp with inventory (weapons, armor, potions), quests (main-story, side-quests) and journal, five text files, and the summary 8 directories, 5 files
session-1-1/fig3-camp-tree.caption: The commands on the left build the tree on the right. mkdir -p builds a whole chain of folders, touch makes an empty file, and the slashes in a path are the branches.

session-1-1/fig4-overwrite-vs-append.alt: Three columns showing day-01.txt after three echo commands: write with a single > leaves one line; append with >> leaves two lines; then a third echo with a single > leaves only its own line in red and the two earlier lines struck through; a strip beneath says one arrow replaces and two arrows add
session-1-1/fig4-overwrite-vs-append.caption: A single > empties the file before writing; >> adds to the end. The trap is a journal entry typed with one arrow instead of two: two lines gone, no warning.

session-1-1/fig5-keyboard-map.alt: A long command line with the cursor in the middle, the left half underlined yellow for Ctrl+U and the right half green for Ctrl+K; below, eleven shortcut rows colour-coded recall, move, edit and control: up and down arrows, Tab, Ctrl+R, Ctrl+A, Ctrl+E, Ctrl+U, Ctrl+K, Ctrl+W, Ctrl+Y, Ctrl+C and Ctrl+L, each with a one-line description
session-1-1/fig5-keyboard-map.caption: The keyboard map. Up-arrow, Tab and Ctrl+C make you faster than the mouse on day one; the editing keys arrive the day a long line annoys you enough.

session-1-2/fig1-filesystem-tree.alt: Left, the filesystem drawn as one tree from the root slash: bin, etc, home with adventurer inside it (Desktop leading down to navigation-practice, dungeon, floor-2 and boss-room; Documents; projects), tmp, usr and var, each with a short note; right, the same boss-room reached by an absolute path starting at slash and by a relative path starting with dot-dot from projects, and a legend for slash, tilde, dot, dot-dot and dash
session-1-2/fig1-filesystem-tree.caption: The filesystem is one tree. An absolute path starts at the root and works from anywhere; a relative path starts where you are standing. Both reach the same door.

session-1-2/fig2-reading-ls-la.alt: Top, one line of ls -la pulled apart into columns with a label and meaning under each: d for type, rwxr-xr-x for permissions, 5 links, adventurer owner, staff group, 160 size, Aug 9 10:30 modified, my-folder name; bottom left, a six-line listing with the dot-files dimmed and an executable script in green; bottom right, the flags -l -a -la -lh -lt -lS -R -1 with one-line meanings
session-1-2/fig2-reading-ls-la.caption: ls -la is the status screen. Read a line left to right: type, permissions, links, owner, group, size, date, name. Dot-files are hidden for tidiness, not secrecy.

session-1-2/fig3-pipes-and-redirects.alt: Top, the line ls -la | grep .txt > text-files.txt drawn as a flow: ls -la prints a listing, a green pipe arrow sends it into grep which keeps matching lines, a yellow greater-than arrow sends that into the file; below, three cards for pipe, redirect and append, each with three example commands and what they do
session-1-2/fig3-pipes-and-redirects.caption: Standard output goes to the screen unless you send it somewhere: | into the next command's input, > into a file (replacing it), >> onto the end of a file.

session-1-2/fig4-dungeon-moves.alt: Left, the navigation-practice dungeon drawn as rooms: home above Desktop above navigation-practice above dungeon, which splits into floor-1 (room-a, room-b) and floor-2 (boss-room, the target); right, the eight moves of the drill as rows: where you start, the cd command, and where it lands, colour-coded down a branch, up with dot-dot, absolute or tilde jumps, and dash for back
session-1-2/fig4-dungeon-moves.caption: Every cd is a move on the map. Down a branch with a relative path, up with ., anywhere with an absolute path or ~, and back to the previous room with -.

session-1-2/fig5-permissions.alt: Top, the string -rw-r--r-- split into a type box and three triads labelled owner, group and others with their meanings, plus a key for r, w, x and dash; bottom left, the chmod +x story: ./quest-start.sh gives Permission denied, chmod +x turns -rw-r--r-- into -rwxr-xr-x with the three x highlighted, and the script runs; bottom right, the number system r=4 w=2 x=1 with 755, 644 and 700 explained
session-1-2/fig5-permissions.caption: Who may read, write and run: owner, group, others, three letters each. A new file is never executable; Permission denied on your own script means chmod +x has not happened yet.

session-1-3/fig1-three-states.alt: Three cards side by side: working directory (the field) holding inventory.txt modified, secrets.txt untracked and README.md unchanged; staging area (the waiting room) holding inventory.txt staged; repository (.git) holding three commits; between them the two doors git add and git commit -m with the undo commands underneath, and under each card the lines git status prints for that state
session-1-3/fig1-three-states.caption: Three states, two doors. A file is modified in your folder, staged in the waiting room, or committed in .git; git add and git commit are the only ways through, and git status tells you which room every file is in.

session-1-3/fig2-commit-chain.alt: Left, one commit opened: its forty-character hash, its parent df4829e, author, date, message and the snapshot of every tracked file; right, the four-commit chain as git log --oneline shows it, newest first, each commit pointing down to its parent, with HEAD pointing to main pointing to the newest commit
session-1-3/fig2-commit-chain.caption: A save is a snapshot plus a parent. Every commit holds a whole picture of the folder and the hash of the commit before it; branches are labels on commits, HEAD is the label you are standing on.

session-1-3/fig3-branch-timelines.alt: Top, two timelines leaving the same first commit d1a2a91: main with a dashed next save, side-quest with commit f7b168e and HEAD on it; below, two terminal views of the same folder, one after git checkout side-quest showing side-quest.txt and magic-staff in inventory.txt, one after git checkout main where both are absent
session-1-3/fig3-branch-timelines.caption: One folder, two timelines. checkout rewrites the folder to match the branch you move to; nothing is deleted, the folder is showing a different save.

session-1-3/fig4-two-merges.alt: Left, a fast-forward: main sits behind side-quest on a straight line and after the merge the main label has simply moved up to the same commit, with the Updating and Fast-forward lines git prints; right, a three-way merge: main and dragon-slayer both moved since the fork, so the merge creates a new commit with two parents, with the Merge made by the ort strategy line and the CONFLICT line that appears when both sides changed the same lines
session-1-3/fig4-two-merges.caption: Two shapes of merge. When main never moved, git fast-forwards the label; when both sides moved, git makes a merge commit with two parents, and asks you only if the same lines changed on both.

session-1-3/fig5-conflict-markers.alt: Left, quests.txt after a conflict: the <<<<<<< HEAD marker, two lines from your branch, the ======= fence, two lines from dragon-slayer, the >>>>>>> dragon-slayer marker, each region labelled; right, the three moves that end a conflict: edit until only the file you want remains, git add the file, git commit, plus git merge --abort as the escape hatch
session-1-3/fig5-conflict-markers.caption: Reading a conflict. Git wrote both versions into the file with fences around them; you edit until only the version you want is left, then add and commit.

session-1-4/fig1-local-and-remote.alt: Two boxes: your machine (the working directory ~/git-quest, the full history in ~/git-quest/.git, the main label) and github.com, a remote named origin (adventurer-dev/git-quest, origin/main, the SSH address); between them three arrows: git push going up, git pull coming down, git clone for the first copy; under them the two lines git remote -v prints
session-1-4/fig1-local-and-remote.caption: Local and remote. The whole repository is on your machine; GitHub holds a second copy named origin, and three verbs move commits between them.

session-1-4/fig2-ssh-handshake.alt: Two key cards: the private key ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 in red, never shared, permissions 600; the public key ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub in green, one line pasted into GitHub Settings; below, the four-step handshake on every push: you offer the fingerprint, GitHub sends a challenge, the private key signs it, GitHub checks the signature with the public key; the ssh -T output ending in Hi adventurer-dev
session-1-4/fig2-ssh-handshake.caption: The SSH key pair. The public key is the padlock you hand to GitHub; the private key stays home and answers a challenge on every push.

session-1-4/fig3-push-pull-cycle.alt: Five chips in a row: git pull, edit, git add, git commit, git push, with a loop arrow back to pull; below, a red card showing the rejected push ( ! [rejected] main -> main (fetch first) ) with a two-lane sketch where origin has commit B and you have commit C from the same A, and a green card showing the fix: git pull merges B and C into M, git push sends M
session-1-4/fig3-push-pull-cycle.caption: The daily loop and its one refusal. Pull before you push; when a teammate pushed first, git refuses, you pull, and the merge commit joins both sides.

session-1-4/fig4-pull-request-flow.alt: Top, your own repository: six numbered stages alternating terminal and GitHub: checkout -b, push -u, Compare & pull request, Files changed and Conversation, Merge pull request, then checkout main and pull; a git log --graph showing the merge commit with two parents. Bottom, someone else's repository: push denied, fork to adventurer-dev/quest-board, clone branch push and open a PR that targets the original, maintainers review and merge
session-1-4/fig4-pull-request-flow.caption: A pull request, end to end. On your own repo you merge it; on someone else's you fork first and the maintainers decide.

session-1-4/fig5-dotfiles-anatomy.alt: The dotfiles repository as six rows, each tagged with the Unit 1 session it came from: .zshrc (aliases, welcome line), vscode/settings.json, vscode/extensions.txt, setup.sh, README.md, .gitignore, each with a one-line sample; below, three steps for a new machine: git clone, cd and ./setup.sh, source ~/.zshrc
session-1-4/fig5-dotfiles-anatomy.caption: The dotfiles repo. Every file is a Unit 1 session kept; three commands rebuild the whole environment on a new machine.

session-2-1/fig1-request-cycle.alt: Five steps from pressing Enter to a painted page: you type a URL, DNS turns the name into an IP, the browser sends GET /index.html, the server answers 200 with an HTML file, and the browser parses that file, fetches what it names, and paints. Under them, the request and the response written as the two halves of one exchange.
session-2-1/fig1-request-cycle.caption: The request, then the page. A page is a file a server sent because a browser asked, and drawing it happens after the file arrives.

session-2-1/fig2-document-anatomy.alt: The document every page shares: doctype, html with lang, head, body, and the closing html, each with what it is for. Beside them, the head in yellow (title, charset, viewport, never painted) and the body in green (the words the reader sees), with the warning that head and header are different elements.
session-2-1/fig2-document-anatomy.caption: One document, two audiences. The head is for the browser and is never painted; the body is everything the reader sees.

session-2-1/fig3-semantic-skeleton.alt: The same page drawn twice. Left, seven nested divs with class names (top, links, wrapper, box, side, bottom) that mean nothing to a screen reader. Right, the named skeleton: header, nav, main containing section and article, aside, and footer, each with the job it does.
session-2-1/fig3-semantic-skeleton.caption: Name the region, or it is just a box. Semantic elements say what a region is; a div says nothing, and is what you use when no named element fits.

session-2-1/fig4-element-shapes.alt: Three cards: a paired element with an opening tag, content and a closing tag; void elements with no close tag (img, br, hr, meta, input); attributes as name equals quoted value on the opening tag only. Below, the heading outline from h1 to h4 indented, and the rule that a heading level is depth, not a font size.
session-2-1/fig4-element-shapes.caption: Three shapes, and an outline. Most elements are a pair, a few hold nothing, attributes live on the opening tag, and heading levels are not a size knob.

session-2-1/fig5-form-wiring.alt: Four rows showing a label's for attribute matching a control's id: email input, class select, bio textarea, and a terms checkbox. Beside them, what each input type does (text, email, tel, url, password, date, radio) and the required attribute, with the browser's own message, Please fill out this field.
session-2-1/fig5-form-wiring.caption: A form is a set of matching names. The label's for and the control's id are the same string, the type picks the check, and required is the browser refusing an empty send.

session-2-2/fig1-rule-homes.alt: A CSS rule with a selector and two declarations, then the three places a rule can live: an inline style attribute marked as the worst, a style tag in the head marked as only for a test, and an external style.css linked from the head marked as the one to keep.
session-2-2/fig1-rule-homes.caption: A rule, and the three places it can live. The selector names the elements; the declarations give the orders; the file linked from the head is where the orders stay.

session-2-2/fig2-specificity-ladder.alt: Four competing rules for one paragraph, scored as columns rather than a sum: the element selector, the class, the id which wins, and an inline style which would beat the id. Below, a tie broken by source order, and the !important trapdoor.
session-2-2/fig2-specificity-ladder.caption: Which rule wins. Compare the columns from the left, ids then classes then elements; a tie goes to the later rule, and !important is how that system stops working.

session-2-2/fig3-box-model.alt: The four layers of an element nested: margin outside and unpainted, then border, then padding which is painted, then content. Beside them the same card measured two ways: content-box makes 300 plus padding plus border equal 346, and border-box keeps the box at 300.
session-2-2/fig3-box-model.caption: Every element is a box. Padding is inside and painted, margin is outside and empty, and border-box makes the width you wrote the width you get.

session-2-2/fig4-selector-map.alt: The about page from the previous session, header and navigation and a centered card and a footer, beside the selector that paints each region: header, nav a, nav a:hover, a group of headings, p.intro, an id, and a reusable class.
session-2-2/fig4-selector-map.caption: Aim the selector. A class is reusable and weak, a descendant hits only what is inside, and an id is stronger than you want for a color.

session-2-2/fig5-custom-properties.alt: A :root list of named tokens, primary, accent, background, surface, a heading font and a spacing step, each with a swatch, and arrows to the rules that call them with var(): the header, the headings, links and prices, the body, and the section.
session-2-2/fig5-custom-properties.caption: Name the value once. Change the accent token and every rule that calls it moves, because the decision lives in one place.

session-2-3/fig1-flex-axes.alt: Two flex rows of three chips. The left is flex-direction row: justify-content moves the chips left and right, align-items moves them up and down. The right is flex-direction column: the same two properties swap axes.
session-2-3/fig1-flex-axes.caption: One axis, then the other. justify-content follows the main axis, align-items follows the cross axis, and flex-direction decides which way those words point.

session-2-3/fig4-mobile-first.alt: The same five regions three times. With no query they stack: header, nav, main, aside, footer. At min-width 768 the nav sits beside main and aside. At min-width 1024 the full holy grail appears, nav and aside flanking main.
